source.title: AI Model Utilization Measurements For Finding Class Encoding Patterns
source.authors: P. Bajcsy; A. Cardone; Chenyi Ling; Philippe Dessauw; Michael Majurski; Timothy Blattner; Derek Juba; Walid Keyrouz

record.tranche_reason: The study measures activation-state patterns at computation-graph nodes and explicitly characterizes one layer as poly-semantic, using utilization and tensor-state analysis rather than the original feature-visualization method. It does not test individual neurons directly.
record.gate_note: The authors' discussion of poly-semantic neurons in prior work is background, not a result. The study's own result directly relevant to polysemanticity is its analysis of shared and class-specific tensor-state characteristics at layer1.2.conv2 for two clean traffic-sign classes. Other utilization results concern Trojan detection or triggered inputs and do not measure the claim versions' polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. Its only use of the term is a remark that one whole layer, layer1.2.conv2 (64 channels, binarized jointly into tensor-states), is "poly-semantic". The reason given is that it carries both shared background features and class-specific traffic-sign features for two classes. That describes a multi-channel layer's joint code, not individual neurons responding to unrelated inputs. No neuron-level measure of polysemanticity, share or cause is reported. The paper's results concern utilization fingerprints and Trojan (clean vs poisoned) encodings.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors' main conclusions concern Trojans. A poisoned model gives completely independent tensor-states for clean versus poisoned images of the same class. Utilization patterns in subgraphs change under poisoning and could coarsely indicate tampering. Fingerprints help narrow which subgraphs to inspect. Common class tensor-states come from both foreground and background. The poly-semantic remark about layer1.2.conv2 is a side observation.
record.recipe_differences: The study binarizes node outputs at zero and analyzes tensor-state distributions and utilization; it does not use the original source's neuron feature-visualization procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported utilization patterns vary with the evaluated class and with clean versus poisoned or triggered image sets; the paper also describes variability across training replicates.

fits_no_version.finding: At ResNet101 layer1.2.conv2, two clean traffic-sign classes share high-frequency joint tensor-states for background (blue sky, saturated regions). Foreground sign tensor-states barely overlap (Table 4, Figs 9-10). The authors call the layer poly-semantic on this basis.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early convolutional layers jointly encode class-shared background features and class-specific foreground features in their binarized activation patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: In a poisoned ResNet101, clean and Kelvin-filtered images of the same class share only 35 high-frequency tensor-state values at layer1.2.conv2. Entropy utilization is 33 vs 30.6 (Table 6, Figs 22-23).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A pixel-wide trigger transformation yields largely disjoint layer-level activation-state encodings for inputs with the same semantic label.

record.problems: The polysemanticity example covers one layer and two related traffic-sign classes, not individual neurons or unrelated semantic categories. The authors state that they did not perform quality evaluations of explainability using model-parameter and data-randomization tests. The clean and poisoned evaluation images were not matched pairs differing only by the trigger.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported utilization results compare clean and poisoned models or triggered inputs for Trojan-analysis purposes; they do not measure the polysemanticity versions. No additional qualifying polysemanticity results were reported.

untested.parts: All of it: no individual-neuron responses, no unrelated-category mixtures, no feature visualization.
All; no superposition or capacity analysis of neurons.
All; no comparison of polysemantic share across architectures or activations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's fits_no_version entry cited a nonexistent row R3; it is re-entered here with no row ids. The study is not an original source. Its 'poly-semantic' usage applies Olah et al.'s neuron-level term to a whole layer's joint binarized code. A 64-channel layer encoding multiple features is expected and does not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The analysis is at a computation-unit/layer level, not individual neurons; it compares two related traffic-sign classes rather than unrelated categories such as cats and cars, and does not measure strong responses.
Language models, MLP neurons, and token/context polysemanticity.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or feature-capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Changes in the share of polysemantic neurons due to architecture, activation, or regularization, and performance costs of reducing that share.
Whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect one shared feature or related features rather than unrelated inputs.
Whether polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: ResNet101
rows.operation_detail: Counted unique binarized tensor-state values and calculated entropy-based utilization at layer1.2.conv2 for clean class images.
rows.measure: Unique tensor-state values above frequency thresholds and entropy-based utilization
rows.note: The authors characterize the layer as poly-semantic because it constructs common and unique class characteristics. The classes are both traffic signs, so this does not establish responses to unrelated categories or individual-neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Counts of unique joint tensor-states and entropy utilization for a 64-channel layer across two classes cannot show whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The layer label is the authors' loose use of the term, not a measurement of V1. The 'partial' state and V1 link should be removed.

rows.subject: ResNet101
rows.operation_detail: Compared tensor-state values at one computation unit across images from two clean classes.
rows.measure: Spatial overlap and class-common versus class-specific tensor-state characteristics
rows.value: The text reports common tensor-state values corresponding to blue sky and saturated regions, while the foreground traffic-sign features were distinct apart from a small number of white pixels.
rows.locator: Section 4.2.2, Figures 9 and 10 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors call layer1.2.conv2 poly-semantic in this comparison. The shared and distinct characteristics are described for traffic-sign classes; the study does not establish that they are unrelated semantic inputs.
rows.check: Spatial overlap of high-frequency tensor-states (sky/saturated background shared, sign foreground distinct) is at layer level, for two related traffic-sign classes. It does not measure single-neuron responses to unrelated categories, so it does not bear on V1.

relation.reason: The study borrows the poly-semantic/mono-semantic terms from Olah and Räuker for one layer and for subgraphs, without testing them.

tranche.reason: The text applies the poly-semantic label to a whole layer only in passing. It reports no test of any version.

source_check.notes: Here 'poly-semantic' is a layer-level remark about 64 jointly binarized channels, made for two related traffic-sign classes. It is not a per-neuron result. The Table 4 caption also mentions poisoned images, but the columns are clean classes 32 and 33.

reader_labels.reason: The authors report shared and class-specific characteristics at the same computation unit and explicitly characterize it as poly-semantic; this supports a layer-level version of the claim in this tested setting, not its individual-neuron or unrelated-category examples (R1, R2).
